title: Climate change is driving a ‘shift’ in childhood malaria risk across Africa - Carbon Brief
gist: A Nature study by Carlson et al. applies climate attribution to malaria for the first time, finding warming has added just one childhood case per 1,000 in sub-Saharan Africa since 1900 while sharply redistributing risk - up 8+ cases per 1,000 in the Ethiopian highlands, down four per 1,000 in western Africa. The headline investor-relevant finding is that public health policy has moved malaria roughly 200 times more than climate change has.

themes.theme: First climate attribution applied to an infectious disease

insights.claim: The study is the first to use climate attribution methods - comparing a modelled world with global warming to one without - to quantify climate change's effect on malaria, and is described as the most comprehensive look to date at climate change's impact on any infectious disease.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Attribution science is expanding from extreme weather into health outcomes, creating a new evidentiary basis for climate-related health liability, insurance pricing and adaptation funding claims.
insights.locator: The lead author tells Carbon Brief

insights.claim: The analysis rests on an unusually rare asset: more than 50,000 blood samples collected across sub-Saharan Africa over 1900-2016 and assembled in 2017, stretching back before human-caused warming was strongly felt.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The method is only replicable where century-scale disease datasets exist - expect attribution-for-health to be data-gated, favouring diseases and regions with colonial-era record keeping.
insights.locator: The size and quality of the malaria dataset

insights.claim: The authors built a statistical model separating climatic from social and economic drivers - temperature, rainfall, economic development, healthcare and population - before coupling it to climate models to simulate past and future malaria.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: This separation of climate from development signal is the analytical template likely to be applied to other climate-health impact claims; scrutinise whether socioeconomic controls are present.
insights.locator: The authors use the blood test survey

insights.claim: The link between climate change and malaria in Africa has been surprisingly contentious, with over a dozen studies arguing for or against climate change as a substantial driver of east African highland malaria resurgence.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: A long-running scientific dispute is now being closed - watch for the finding to reshape donor narratives and WHO/Global Fund allocation arguments.
insights.quote: malaria resurgence in the east African highlands became a particular point of contention
insights.locator: The link between climate change and malaria

insights.claim: Lead author Colin Carlson claims the paper is the first study to confidently answer the highland East Africa debate and represents the most clarity yet on the malaria question.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Watch whether east African health ministries and donors reweight highland surveillance budgets on the back of this finding.
insights.quote: I think it’s the most clarity we’ve had on the malaria question.
insights.locator: Lead author Carlson says this paper

insights.claim: Independent researcher Teresa Yamana of Columbia University calls the methodology rigorous and says it demonstrates the potential of climate attribution methods to quantify climate impacts on infectious diseases generally.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: External validation increases the odds this method becomes standard, broadening the class of climate-health claims that can be quantified and litigated.
insights.locator: Dr Teresa Yamana, an associate research scientist

themes.theme: Temperature optimum drives geographic redistribution, not aggregate increase

insights.claim: Childhood malaria prevalence peaks when average monthly temperatures reach 24.9C and falls off in both warmer and cooler climates, making the effect of warming dependent on a region's current baseline temperature.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The 24.9C optimum is the key parameter: it converts a global temperature forecast into a directional, region-by-region malaria signal for health-system and pharma demand planning.
insights.locator: They find that malaria prevalence in children peaks

insights.claim: Climate change is moving malaria rather than uniformly worsening or improving it, with relief in today's hotspots and new risk nearly everywhere else, according to study author Tamma Carleton of UC Berkeley.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Redistribution rather than escalation means the investable signal is in shifting geography of demand for nets, diagnostics and antimalarials, not in aggregate market growth.
insights.quote: Whether a place sees elevated malaria risks or reduced burdens under climate change depends on how hot it is today. We see relief in the hotspots and new risk nearly everywhere else.
insights.locator: The findings show that

insights.claim: In the Ethiopian highlands, where cold historically limited mosquitoes, childhood malaria rates have risen by more than eight cases per 1,000 children since 1900 as warming expanded mosquito habitat, with a similar increase in cooler southern African countries.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Highland east Africa and cooler southern Africa are the emerging-exposure zones where malaria control infrastructure is weakest relative to new risk.
insights.locator: For example, in the Ethiopian highlands

insights.claim: In western Africa, warming has already cut malaria by about four cases per 1,000 children a year as of 2014, reducing prevalence by 1-2%.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: A rare quantified case of warming reducing a disease burden - useful counterweight when assessing blanket claims that climate change worsens all health outcomes.

insights.claim: Across sub-Saharan Africa as a whole, climate change has added only one extra case of malaria per 1,000 children since 1900, a strikingly small net effect relative to the regional shifts underneath it.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The aggregate number is near-zero while local swings are large - continent-level averages are useless for allocating health resources or assessing exposure.
insights.locator: Overall, climate change has resulted in one extra case

insights.claim: Drought reduces malaria prevalence one to two months later and floods raise it two to three months later, but rainfall is less important than temperature in predicting malaria rates.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Temperature, not precipitation, is the leading indicator to monitor for malaria-driven health demand - flood-linked spikes carry a two-to-three month lead time for response planning.
insights.locator: Mosquitoes also need stagnant or slow-moving water

insights.claim: Under the intermediate SSP2-4.5 scenario, broadly in line with current climate policies, warming is projected to cut childhood malaria by about three cases per 1,000 in central Africa and 16 per 1,000 in west Africa by the end of the century.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: West and central Africa are structurally declining malaria markets under current policy trajectories - relevant to long-horizon global health funding and product demand forecasts.
insights.locator: The study concludes that under the intermediate scenario

insights.claim: Under the same intermediate scenario, malaria could rise about 20% in the Rift Valley and coastal southern Africa - some 30 additional cases per 1,000 children.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The Rift Valley and coastal southern Africa are the highest-growth malaria exposure zones this century; surveillance capacity there is the gap to watch.
insights.locator: By contrast, cases could increase by around 20%

insights.claim: The averted-malaria effect scales with warming: about one case per 1,000 children averted by 2100 under low emissions versus 20 cases per 1,000 - a 9% reduction - under the very-high emissions scenario.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Higher emissions paradoxically lower average African malaria burden, a perverse result that complicates simple climate-health cost-benefit framings used in policy advocacy.
insights.locator: Under the low emissions scenario

themes.theme: Policy dominates climate as the driver of malaria

insights.claim: Climate change is not the primary driver of malaria dynamics: public health measures and government policy have a substantially larger impact on shifting malaria risk in Africa.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Interventions, not emissions pathways, determine malaria outcomes - malaria investment cases should be judged on delivery capacity rather than climate scenarios.

insights.claim: Malaria prevalence fell about 16 percentage points over 2000-15 after the disease was made a target of the Millennium Development Goals - a reduction Carlson says is 200 times greater than the increase attributable to climate change so far.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: A 200:1 ratio of policy effect to climate effect is the single most actionable number here: funding withdrawal from malaria programmes is a far bigger risk than warming.

insights.claim: Carlson argues it would not be tremendously hard both to keep malaria out of new places and to eliminate it where climate change gives it an assist.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The author frames elimination as tractable and cheap relative to the shifting risk - supportive of continued Global Fund-style spending and of vector-control and diagnostics providers.
insights.quote: It would not be tremendously hard both to keep malaria out of new places and to eliminate it where it is maybe going to get a little bit of an assist from climate change.
insights.locator: This reduction is 200 times greater

insights.claim: Carlson explicitly rejects reading declining average malaria as good news, noting climate change will bring a wide range of other negative health impacts that strain healthcare systems.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Guard against the contrarian misreading of this paper; net health-system stress from warming still rises even where malaria falls.
insights.quote: A world that is too hot for malaria is not a good world for the health of children.
insights.locator: Carlson emphasises that this does not mean

insights.claim: Malaria remains a large baseline burden: the WHO estimates 610,000 deaths in 2024, with Africa accounting for 95% of cases and deaths and children under five making up three-quarters of African malaria deaths.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable burden that policy, not climate, controls - and concentrates it almost entirely in African paediatric populations.
insights.locator: Malaria kills hundreds of thousands of people

insights.claim: Forty-two countries, mainly in Europe and the Americas, have eliminated malaria entirely through insecticides, draining breeding swamplands and improving basic healthcare, and global malaria mortality fell 90% over the 20th century.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Elimination is a solved engineering problem in 42 countries - the constraint in Africa is financing and delivery, not technology.
insights.locator: However, malaria is preventable

insights.claim: Janey Messina of the University of Oxford cautions the findings should not be read as forecasts of total future malaria burden, because the models exclude social, demographic and public-health determinants such as inequality, migration, conflict and access to interventions.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The projections isolate the climate channel only; conflict and aid disruption could swamp the modelled climate effect in either direction.
insights.quote: should not be interpreted as forecasts of total future malaria burden

insights.claim: Messina argues the paper's most important message is that effective surveillance, prevention and treatment remain substantially more influential and more actionable than climate change alone.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: An independent expert reframing the study as a case for health-system spending rather than climate spending - watch how donors and NGOs use this framing.
insights.quote: effective surveillance, prevention and treatment remain substantially more influential – and more actionable – than climate change alone.

insights.claim: Adugna Woyessa of the Ethiopian Public Health Institute says the study could bring a paradigm shift in malaria elimination efforts and serve as a tool for engaging giant development partners, while stressing future work must situate global trends in local contexts.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Framing the paper as a fundraising instrument for development partners suggests near-term use in donor advocacy rather than operational planning.
